title: Tangent Lie functor of affine algebraic groups and extension of fields
statement: Let $k$ be any field [def-weil-field] and let $G,H$ be affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], with identities $e_G,e_H$. Put $\mathfrak g=T_{G/k,e_G}$ and $\mathfrak h=T_{H/k,e_H}$ [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space]. These finite-dimensional vector spaces carry canonical Lie brackets [def-wf-lie-algebra]. For a homomorphism $f:G\to H$, the tangent map $df$ is $k$-linear, preserves brackets, and satisfies $d(f'\circ f)=df'\circ df$ whenever $f':H\to J$ is another such homomorphism. Under the identification of tangent vectors with $\ker(G(k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2))\to G(k))$ [def-sc-dual-numbers], write $t_X$ for the point corresponding to $X\in\mathfrak g$. For $G=\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$ [def-sc-general-linear-group], this identification is $t_A=I_n+\epsilon A$ for $A\in\operatorname{Mat}_n(k)$, and the bracket is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Thus a rational representation $r:G\to\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$ satisfies $r(t_X)=I_n+\epsilon dr(X)$. For every field extension $K/k$, there is a canonical isomorphism $K\otimes_k\mathfrak g\cong\operatorname{Lie}(G_K)$ of $K$-Lie algebras, natural in homomorphisms $G\to H$. Here $G_K=G\times_{\operatorname{Spec}k}\operatorname{Spec}K$ is scalar extension and the tensor bracket is $[a\otimes X,b\otimes Y]=ab\otimes[X,Y]$. For the general linear group this isomorphism is entrywise extension of matrices. Neither perfectness nor smoothness nor reducedness is assumed.

source.place: Sections 10.6--10.7, printed p.188; 10.11, p.189; 10.19--10.22 and Theorem 10.23, pp.192--193. In 10.19 take R=K for field-extension compatibility.

proof.text: For each of $G,H$, put $C=k[G]$ and $I=\ker\varepsilon$. The coordinate-Hopf theorem [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf] supplies $\Delta,\varepsilon,S$ with precisely the bialgebra identities required below. The coordinate algebra is finitely generated by [lem-pc-affine-finite-type-algebra]. Under the affine spectrum equivalence [def-weil-affine-spectrum], a homomorphism $f:G\to H$ induces $u=f^*:k[H]\to k[G]$. Pulling back the multiplication and identity diagrams gives $\Delta_Gu=(u\otimes u)\Delta_H$ and $\varepsilon_Gu=\varepsilon_H$. In particular $u(I_H)\subseteq I_G$.

source.place: 10.6, p.188; 10.28--10.29, pp.195--196; coordinate coalgebra preceding Proposition 10.28

proof.text: By [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space] and [def-weil-affine-spectrum], a tangent vector at the specified identity is exactly an algebra map $t:C\to k[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2$ reducing to $\varepsilon$. Write it uniquely as $t(c)=\varepsilon(c)+\epsilon v(c)$. Comparing coefficients in $t(ab)=t(a)t(b)$ says that $v$ is linear and $v(ab)=\varepsilon(a)v(b)+v(a)\varepsilon(b)$. Conversely this condition makes the displayed formula an algebra map with the prescribed reduction. Tangent addition and scaling from [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space] add and scale the coefficients $v$, so this is a linear identification. The restriction assertion of [lem-sfb-bialgebra-distribution-tangent-calculus] then identifies this space $L(C)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_k(I/I^2,k)$. This also identifies its underlying set with the kernel of reduction on group-valued points.

Choose algebra generators $c_1,\ldots,c_s$ of $C$, using [lem-pc-affine-finite-type-algebra], and put $z_i=c_i-\varepsilon(c_i)$. Every element of $C$ is a polynomial in the $z_i$; modulo the ideal generated by the $z_iz_j$, it is a scalar plus a linear combination of the $z_i$. Thus the classes of the $z_i$ span $I/I^2$. Choose a basis using [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-free]; a linearly independent family in the span of $s$ vectors has at most $s$ elements, by finite elimination. If its basis is $(b_1,\ldots,b_d)$, the coordinate functionals form a basis of its dual: every $v$ is $\sum_jv(b_j)b_j^*$. Hence the tangent space is finite-dimensional. This includes $s=0$ and $d=0$.

Apply [lem-sfb-bialgebra-distribution-tangent-calculus] to the coordinate bialgebra from step 1. It makes $L(C)$ a Lie algebra with $[v,w]=v*w-w*v$, where $(v*w)(c)=(v\otimes w)\Delta(c)$. Transfer this bracket through the linear identification of step 2. This construction uses only the given multiplication and identity of $G$, with no choices. Equivalently it is the bracket of invariant derivations under the same cited theorem's bijection $v\mapsto(1\otimes v)\Delta$. Thus it gives the canonical tangent Lie bracket in every characteristic, including nonreduced groups.

For $f$ and $u=f^*$ from step 1, postcomposition of tangent points sends the coefficient $v$ to $v\circ u$, directly by the formula of step 2. It is linear. For $c\in k[H]$, the Hopf-map identity of step 1 gives $((v\circ u)*(w\circ u))(c)=(v\otimes w)((u\otimes u)\Delta_H(c))=(v*w)(u(c))$. Subtracting the equality with $v,w$ interchanged proves bracket preservation by the convolution formula [lem-sfb-bialgebra-distribution-tangent-calculus]. Precomposition by the identity is the identity, and $v\circ(u\circ u')=(v\circ u)\circ u'$, proving the claimed composition law. All maps are the tangent maps of [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space].

source.place: 10.19 equation (59), p.192; 10.21--10.23, pp.192--193; invariant-derivation formulation, p.196

proof.text: For $G=\mathrm{GL}_{n,k}$ use its coordinate maps and matrix-point interpretation [def-sc-general-linear-group]. A point reducing to the identity is uniquely $I_n+\epsilon A$, and every such matrix is invertible with inverse $I_n-\epsilon A$. Its coefficient functional has $v_A(x_{ij})=A_{ij}$. Since $\Delta(x_{ij})=\sum_r x_{ir}\otimes x_{rj}$, the convolution bracket from step 4 has value $\sum_r(A_{ir}B_{rj}-B_{ir}A_{rj})=(AB-BA)_{ij}$ on $x_{ij}$. A derivation at $\varepsilon$ is determined by these values: the Leibniz rule determines it on polynomials and $v(D^{-1})=-\varepsilon(D)^{-2}v(D)$ follows by applying the rule to $DD^{-1}=1$. Therefore the bracket is $AB-BA$. Step 5 applied to $r:G\to\mathrm{GL}_{n,k}$ now gives $r(t_X)=I_n+\epsilon dr(X)$.

source.place: 10.7 and 10.11, pp.188--189; Theorem 10.23, p.193; matrix check requested after Proposition 10.29, p.196

proof.text: Let $K/k$ be a field extension. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], $G_K$ has coordinate ring $C_K=K\otimes_kC$. Its counit is $a\otimes c\mapsto a\varepsilon(c)$ and its comultiplication sends $a\otimes c$ to $\sum(a\otimes c_{(1)})\otimes_K(1\otimes c_{(2)})$, by pulling back the group diagrams. Write $I_K=\ker\varepsilon_K$. Flatness of $K$ over $k$ [lem-weil-pbc-module-over-field-flat] and tensor exactness [lem-weil-pbc-flat-tensor-exact] identify $K\otimes_k I$ with $I_K$ inside $C_K$. Products of elements $a\otimes i$ and $b\otimes j$ equal $ab\otimes ij$, and conversely $a\otimes ij=(a\otimes i)(1\otimes j)$; hence $I_K^2$ is the image of $K\otimes_k I^2$. Tensor right exactness [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-right-exact] applied to $I^2\to I\to I/I^2\to0$ therefore gives the canonical isomorphism $K\otimes_k(I/I^2)\simeq I_K/I_K^2$, sending $a\otimes\bar i$ to $a\otimes i\bmod I_K^2$.

source.place: 10.19, p.192, with R=K; Stacks Tags 01I4 (affine fibre product), 00HD (flat tensor exactness)

proof.text: The space $V=I/I^2$ has a basis $(b_1,\ldots,b_d)$ by step 3 [def-weil-pbc-free-module], with dual basis $(b_j^*)$ of $V^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,k)$. Define the $K$-linear map $\psi:K\otimes_kV^\vee\to\operatorname{Hom}_K(K\otimes_kV,K)$ by $\psi(a\otimes\lambda)(b\otimes x)=ab\lambda(x)$; it is well defined by bilinearity. Since tensor product commutes with finite direct sums, $(1\otimes b_j)$ is a $K$-basis of $K\otimes_kV$ and $(1\otimes b_j^*)$ a $K$-basis of $K\otimes_kV^\vee$. Also $\psi(1\otimes b_j^*)(1\otimes b_i)=\delta_{ij}$, so $\psi$ sends a basis to the dual basis of a finite basis and is an isomorphism (this includes $d=0$). Together with steps 2 and 7 this gives $\Phi:K\otimes_k\mathfrak g\simeq\operatorname{Lie}(G_K)$, characterized on coefficient derivations by $\Phi(a\otimes v)(b\otimes c)=abv(c)$ (use $v(1)=0$ to pass from $I_K$ to $C_K$). For pure tensors, evaluating the scalar-extended comultiplication from step 7 gives $(\Phi(a\otimes v)*\Phi(b\otimes w))(d\otimes c)=abd(v*w)(c)$. Subtract the reversed product; by step 4, $[\Phi(a\otimes v),\Phi(b\otimes w)]=\Phi(ab\otimes[v,w])$. Bilinearity extends this to finite sums. For $u=f^*$, both naturality composites evaluated on $b\otimes c$ give $abv(u(c))$; thus they agree. For matrices the same formula sends $a\otimes A$ to the matrix with entries $aA_{ij}$, proving entrywise extension. No smoothness, perfectness or reducedness was used.
